title: [Articles] Two-step deep learning for candidemia prediction using time-series electronic health record data from the USA: a model development and validation study
desc: A two-step deep-learning framework integrating candidemia and mortality risk may support early identification of high-risk patients and facilitate timely empiric antifungal therapy. Prospective studies are warranted to confirm the findings.

title: In-context learning for medical artificial intelligence
desc: Wong et al. review how in-context learning enables large language models to adapt to medical tasks using examples rather than model parameter updates. They map its applications and limitations and propose a risk-proportionate framework for evaluation, governance, and monitoring to guide responsible clinical translation.

title: Artificial intelligence for cerebrovascular digital subtraction angiography: methods, evidence, and challenges.
source: PubMed · Physics in medicine and biology
desc: [Physics in medicine and biology] Cerebrovascular diseases remain a major cause of mortality and long-term disability worldwide. Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) provides high-spatiotemporal-resolution visualization of cerebrovascular anatomy and contrast-agent dynamics and plays an important role in diagnosis, interventional treatment planning, and treatment assessment. Artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly been applied to cerebrovascular DSA, yet the available evidence is distributed across diverse imaging settings, technical tasks, datasets, and validation strategies. This structured topical review provides a DSA-centered overview of AI-assisted cerebrovascular image analysis across 2D DSA, three-dimensional rotational angiography, and four-dimensional DSA. Literature from Web of Science Core Collection and major engineering databases was screened at title, abstract, and full-text levels using predefined eligibility criteria. The literature is organized around six interconnected tasks: image preprocessing, vessel and lesion segmentation, image registration, reconstruction and generation, disease diagnosis and detection, and hemodynamic analysis. Representative conventional and learning-based methods are reviewed together with their datasets, evaluation metrics, validation designs, and available data or code resources, with particular attention to the strength and limitations of the supporting evidence. Recent studies demonstrate increasing use of spatiotemporal modeling, deep learning, and image-generation techniques, but clinical translation remains constrained by small or single-center datasets, heterogeneous acquisition protocols and evaluation practices, limited external and prospective validation, model interpretability, and deployment requirements. Future work should emphasize acquisition-aware and physics-informed modeling, multicenter and privacy-preserving collaboration, clinically meaningful validation, and closer integration with neurointerventional workflows. By linking methodological developments with their supporting evidence and translational challenges, this review aims to support the development of more robust and clinically applicable AI methods for cerebrovascular DSA.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted 4D Dynamic Long-Axial PET Imaging for the Detection of Early Pancreatic Cancer Lesions
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Ruijin Hospital; conditions: Pancreas Carcinoma, PDAC - Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 50; status: RECRUITING] Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is associated with a poor prognosis, and early detection of pancreatic lesions is of great importance for improving patient outcomes. In this study, whole-body imaging with FDG and FAPI will be used to visualize the early development of pancreatic cancer lesions from multiple perspectives, including glucose metabolism, tumor fibrotic stroma, and integrin receptor expression. Furthermore, leveraging the advantages of four-dimensional dynamic long-axial PET imaging, artificial intelligence-assisted lesion detection and analysis will be performed to characterize lesions and differentiate between benign and malignant lesions. The imaging findings will subsequently be compared with postoperative histopathological results to evaluate the diagnostic performance of the proposed imaging approaches.

title: SkinMind: Equipping Agentic RAG with Human-Inspired Graph Probing for Reliable Dermatology AI
desc: Reliable dermatology AI requires access to verifiable evidence distributed across heterogeneous textual and visual sources. However, conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically relies on one-shot retrieval from flat corpora, limiting its ability to adapt retrieval granularity, explore multi-hop relations, and integrate multimodal clinical evidence. We introduce SkinMind, a multimodal agentic RAG framework that equips policy models with human-inspired graph probing for autonomous evidence seeking. SkinMind organizes retrieval as an iterative interaction between an orchestrator and a graph environment. Through eight hierarchical graph-probing tools, the orchestrator progressively identifies relevant entities, inspects node-level information, traverses relations and paths, and retrieves source-text and visual evidence. This progressive-disclosure design allows the model to adaptively determine the retrieval modality, exploration direction, and evidence granularity while constructing a query-specific evidence subgraph. To support autonomous graph probing, we construct SkinMind-KG from a 62M-token corpus of dermatology guidelines and textbooks and 423K images, guided by a dermatologist-informed schema and a conflict-resolution mechanism. The resulting graph contains over 1.0M nodes and 2.0M edges, unifying textual, relational, and visual evidence for retrieval. Across six dermatology VQA benchmarks and two policy-model settings, SkinMind improves the average score over direct answering by 8.70 and 8.89 points with GPT-5.4-mini and Gemini-2.5-Flash, respectively, while consistently outperforming competing RAG methods. Together, SkinMind and SkinMind-KG provide an effective foundation for evidence-grounded multimodal reasoning in dermatology.

title: Weight-Space Programming for Medical Imaging: Do We Still Need Training Data?
desc: Can a large language model (LLM) write the parameters of a medical image classifier from medical knowledge alone, without any training data? Such classifiers normally require labelled images, which are costly and often unavailable. We investigate this question through weight-space programming (WSP), in which an LLM writes or adapts the weights and biases of a neural network directly, without optimisation on training data. Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra each generate the parameters of a small LeNet-style CNN in a single reply, without tool use and without access to any image. We compare these networks against zero-shot MedSigLIP and against the same architecture trained on labels using the Adam optimiser, across 7 classification tasks in four modalities: chest X-ray, breast ultrasound and abdominal CT (all from MedMNIST), and pelvic MRI (SynthUterus). The LLM-written networks perform above chance on all six MedMNIST tasks, with a mean test AUC of 0.719 for Opus and 0.711 for Astra. Both models outperform MedSigLIP on 5 of 6 tasks while using more than 10,000 times fewer parameters. However, the same network trained with Adam on only 256 labelled images achieves a higher AUC on every MedMNIST task (mean AUC 0.828). On SynthUterus, Opus attains an AUC of 0.764, whereas Astra falls below chance (AUC 0.136) owing to a systematic error. These results show that LLMs can write functional medical classifiers, but that they do not yet replace training data. We release the protocol, logs and all generated weights at https://github.com/MaximilianLindholz/weight-space-programming-medical.

title: Exploring Data Augmentation for Stroke Severity Prediction: How Generative AI Enhances EEG Signal Classification
desc: In clinical datasets, data augmentation is often avoided because it can remove important unusual values, known as outliers, which are important for understanding diseases accurately. However, clinical EEG datasets often suffer from two key limitations: small sample sizes and class imbalance, which significantly reduce classification performance. To overcome these challenges, this study applies generative AI-based data augmentation techniques with a carefully designed hybrid pipeline that effectively enhances performance even on limited EEG data. Using EEG signals from 50 brain stroke patients, we investigate both traditional oversampling methods (SMOTE and ADASYN) and advanced generative models, including WGAN and WGAN-GP. Our proposed pipeline involves preprocessing EEG recordings, extracting comprehensive statistical and frequency-domain features, applying feature reduction, and evaluating multiple machine learning classifiers. Experimental results show that the combination of SelectKBest feature selection, SVM classifier, and WGAN-GP augmentation achieves the highest classification accuracy of 72%, outperforming other methods. This work introduces a novel hybrid approach for EEG-based stroke severity classification, demonstrating that generative augmentation, when integrated properly, can significantly improve performance on small clinical datasets. To the best of our knowledge, this combination of techniques has not been explored before on any dataset, providing a solid foundation for future research in automated EEG-based stroke diagnosis.

title: LingoCell interprets gene perturbations through natural language and tissue niches
desc: Single-cell foundation models are general tools for resolving cell identities and disease states, but struggle to interpret changes in expression magnitude in biological language, to transfer to sparse spatial measurements, and to explain cellular niches. We introduce LingoCell, a foundation model connecting single-cell and spatial transcriptomics. It aligns cell representations with language while keeping gene expression editable, supporting cell annotation, cross-batch integration, description generation, and disease-language readouts of single-gene and combinatorial in silico perturbations. Extended to tissues, it annotates cells without single-cell references, learns identity-conditioned niche embeddings, and performs spatial in silico perturbation by replacing and editing neighbor expression. In lung adenocarcinoma, LingoCell revealed synergistic disease responses to jointly weakening alveolar differentiation programs and strengthening malignant programs. In colorectal cancer, it revealed different programs conveyed by the same fibroblast state to T cells, macrophages, and tumor cells. LingoCell provides a unified framework for prioritizing target combinations and stromal intervention programs.

Weakly supervised deep learning predicts perineural invasion from H&E whole-slide images in tongue squamous cell carcinoma: development and external validation.
source: PubMed · International journal of medical informatics
desc: [International journal of medical informatics] Perineural invasion (PNI) in tongue squamous cell carcinoma (TSCC) is associated with aggressive behavior and poor outcomes, yet it can be under-recognized on H&E sections because it is often focal and interpretation varies. Manual assessment of PNI suffers from significant interobserver variability, motivating AI-based decision support. We developed and externally validated a weakly supervised WSI model to predict PNI in TSCC. We retrospectively analyzed 1,511 digitized H&E whole-slide images from 629 patients at two centers. Patient-level partitioning yielded an internal training cohort of 305 patients and 787 WSIs, an internal validation cohort of 132 patients and 340 WSIs, and an external test cohort of 192 patients and 384 WSIs. Non-overlapping tiling generated 41,552,500 candidate patches before tissue-background exclusion, of which 7,813,555 unique tissue patches were retained for analysis. A two-stage pipeline was used: patch-level modeling and MIL-based slide aggregation. ResNet50 was selected over Inception_v3 and SimpleViT as the feature extractor. Patch-level prediction probabilities and image features were aggregated into a 101-dimensional patch likelihood histogram (PLH) and a 101-dimensional visual bag-of-words (BoW) representation, respectively. For conventional classifiers, the two representations were concatenated into a 202-dimensional vector, followed by z-score normalization and LASSO feature selection. For the Transformer, the two representations were processed separately using PCA, independently projected into 128-dimensional embedding spaces, and integrated using four-head cross-attention. Performance was assessed by ROC, decision curve analysis (DCA), and calibration. The internal training, internal validation, and external test cohorts included 305, 132, and 192 patients, respectively. PNI prevalence was 82.3%, 79.5%, and 72.9% in these cohorts, respectively. The Transformer fusion model achieved AUCs of 0.990 in the training cohort, 0.968 in the internal validation cohort, and 0.940 in the external test cohort. Calibration and decision curve analysis were used to characterize the model's predicted probabilities and modeled net benefit in the retrospective study cohorts. Patch-level Grad-CAM was used to generate qualitative saliency visualisations associated with ResNet50 patch-level PNI scores. title: LLM-Supported Pain Neuroscience Education for Physiotherapy Students
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: İsmail Palalı; conditions: Pain, Chronic Pain, Health Professions Education; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 120; status: COMPLETED] Physiotherapists need to explain pain to patients in a way that is scientifically accurate, understandable, and non-threatening. Pain neuroscience education (PNE) improves students' pain knowledge, but it is unclear whether this translates into retained ability to explain pain to patients. This randomized controlled trial tested whether adding structured feedback from a large language model (LLM; GPT-5.2 Instant, OpenAI, via the ChatGPT interface) to a standardized four-week PNE programme improves undergraduate physiotherapy students' pain-explanation competence compared with the same programme using standardized expert-developed (non-AI) feedback. The primary outcome was Pain Explanation Competence (PEC) on a previously unseen clinical transfer scenario, assessed without AI access 12 weeks after the intervention by three assessors blinded to group allocation.
